meta.title: Who really said "The past is already gone, the future is not yet here. There's only one moment for you to live"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not the Buddha. It is Thích Nhất Hạnh paraphrasing him. The sutta behind it says “What is past is left behind. The future is as yet unreached” — and stops there.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The past is already gone, the future is not yet here. There's only one moment for you to live'?
meta.ogDescription: A Dharma-talk paraphrase that acquired quotation marks in print. The canonical verse, MN 131, tells you not to chase the past — it never says you have only one moment to live.

answer.label: Not the Buddha — Thích Nhất Hạnh paraphrasing him
answer.authorDates: 1926–2022 · Vietnamese Zen monk, teacher and peace activist
answer.sourceLine: The first half is a fair rendering of a real discourse; the second half is not scripture at all. In the Bhaddekaratta Sutta (MN 131), in Thanissaro Bhikkhu’s translation ↗ the Buddha’s verse runs “You shouldn’t chase after the past or place expectations on the future. What is past is left behind. The future is as yet unreached. Whatever quality is present you clearly see right there, right there.” It says to see the present clearly. It does not say there is only one moment for you to live. That flourish is Thích Nhất Hạnh’s, from talks in which he introduced the thought as something “the Buddha said that…” — a reporting clause the printed versions dropped.

source.heading: The discourse, and what was added to it

docMeta.dd: Thanissaro Bhikkhu, “An Auspicious Day,” Access to Insight
Thích Nhất Hạnh, in Dharma talks and books published under his name
Breathe, You Are Alive — which Bodhipaksa dates to 2008

source.excerpt: You shouldn’t chase after the past or place expectations on the future. What is past is left behind. The future is as yet unreached. Whatever quality is present you clearly see right there, right there. Not taken in, unshaken, that’s how you develop the heart.
trail: The Buddha’s verse in MN 131, “An Auspicious Day” ↗ reads in full: “You shouldn’t chase after the past or place expectations on the future. What is past is left behind. The future is as yet unreached. Whatever quality is present you clearly see right there, right there.” The first two clauses of the popular quote track it closely; the third has no counterpart.

Bodhipaksa’s Fake Buddha Quotes entry on this line (archived 17 August 2025) ↗ calls it fake and gives the reason in one sentence: “There’s only one moment for you to live” is “far too metaphorical and poetic for the language of the Pali canon.” He identifies the Bhaddekaratta Sutta as the scriptural model.

The same page reconstructs how it turned into a quotation: in talks Thích Nhất Hạnh said things like “The Buddha said that the past is already gone…”, and Bodhipaksa reports that in later books — he names “2008’s Breathe, You Are Alive” — the line follows “The Buddha said” and is set in quotation marks ↗ — the same lost-reporting-clause mechanism he documents on several other Nhất Hạnh lines.

The Internet Archive’s catalogue record for Breathe! You Are Alive ↗ covers the book; the copy scanned there is a Parallax Press revised edition catalogued as 1996, not the 2008 printing Bodhipaksa names, so no page is confirmed here.
source.excerptNote: The sutta’s verse, run together as prose. The instruction is to see present experience clearly and stay unshaken by it — a different claim from “there’s only one moment for you to live,” which reads the verse as a statement about how much life you have rather than about where to put your attention.

author.name: Thích Nhất Hạnh
author.heading: Who Thích Nhất Hạnh was
author.metaLine: 1926–2022 · Vietnamese Zen monk, teacher and peace activist
author.bio: Thích Nhất Hạnh spent thirty-nine years exiled from Vietnam for refusing to take a side in its war, and built at Plum Village in France a community whose main export was talk — hundreds of Dharma talks a year, given in English to mixed audiences and then transcribed into books. He was a genuinely great populariser of early Buddhist material, which is why so many of the lines pinned on the Buddha online turn out to be his: the summaries were good enough to sound canonical.

copyAttribution: "The past is already gone, the future is not yet here. There's only one moment for you to live." — Not the Buddha. The wording is Thích Nhất Hạnh's, given in Dharma talks as reported speech and later printed inside quotation marks. The canonical model is the Bhaddekaratta Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya 131), whose verse reads, in Thanissaro Bhikkhu's translation: "What is past is left behind. The future is as yet unreached. Whatever quality is present you clearly see right there, right there." Traced by Quotle.info.

misattribution.heading: Two-thirds scripture, one-third flourish
misattribution.intro: The quote is not made up out of nothing. It is a real teaching with a memorable line welded on, and the weld is where the attribution fails.

items.why: The sentence appears in no Pali discourse. Bodhipaksa’s objection is stylistic as well as textual ↗: “There’s only one moment for you to live” is, he writes, “far too metaphorical and poetic for the language of the Pali canon,” which is formulaic and repetitive by design.

items.who: Thích Nhất Hạnh, in Dharma talks
items.why: He introduced the thought as reported speech — “The Buddha said that the past is already gone…” — which is a summary, not a citation. The reporting clause disappears in the printed version ↗, and with it the signal that these are the paraphraser’s words.

items.tag: Modern phrasing, not a canonical line
items.why: MN 131 ↗ tells you not to chase the past or place expectations on the future, and to see present experience clearly without being taken in by it. Reading that as “there’s only one moment for you to live” is an interpretation — a defensible one, but an interpretation, and the sutta never makes the claim itself.

misattribution.truthLine: What the Buddha is recorded as saying, in the Bhaddekaratta Sutta ↗, is quieter and more practical: “You shouldn’t chase after the past or place expectations on the future… Whatever quality is present you clearly see right there, right there. Not taken in, unshaken, that’s how you develop the heart.”

context.heading: Why the flourish is the giveaway
lead: The Pali discourses were composed to be memorised and chanted by people who had no writing. That gives them a very particular texture: stock phrases, exhaustive lists, whole paragraphs repeated verbatim with one noun swapped. It is superb mnemonic engineering and it is nobody’s idea of quotable prose. A line that lands in eleven crisp words is, on style alone, evidence of a modern hand.

The Bhaddekaratta Sutta is also not really about seizing the day. Thanissaro Bhikkhu notes in his introduction that bhaddekaratta was probably a pre-Buddhist term the Buddha adopted and re-interpreted — the point being that your own attitude to time, rather than stars or omens, is what makes a day auspicious. The discourse then spends most of its length on a technical analysis of how one “chases after the past” through the five aggregates. It is a meditation instruction, not a memento mori.
context.detailsSummary: What the sutta actually walks through
detailsBody: After the verse, the Buddha defines each of its terms in turn: chasing after the past means delighting in “in the past I had such a form… such a feeling… such a perception… such a thought-fabrication… such a consciousness”; placing expectations on the future is the same list in the future tense. The full analysis is in the discourse ↗.

Being “taken in with regard to present qualities” is then defined as seeing form as self, or self as possessing form, and so on through all five aggregates. None of this is about the shortness of life. It is about not identifying with experience as it arises — which is why the closing line of the verse is “not taken in, unshaken,” not “you have only this moment.”
context.pull: Eleven crisp words are not how the Pali canon talks.

sourcesVerified.claim: Bodhipaksa calls the quote fake, says the third clause is too metaphorical for the Pali canon, names the Bhaddekaratta Sutta as its model, and reports it printed as a quotation in the 2008 Breathe, You Are Alive.

MN 131 in Thanissaro Bhikkhu's translation reads "You shouldn't chase after the past or place expectations on the future. What is past is left behind. The future is as yet unreached. Whatever quality is present you clearly see right there, right there."
The Internet Archive holds a catalogue record for Breathe! You Are Alive by Thích Nhất Hạnh (Parallax printing catalogued 1996).
Wikipedia gives Thích Nhất Hạnh's dates as 11 October 1926 – 22 January 2022 and describes his years of exile.
